title: Measuring your results
desc: Compare your results with the right benchmark, after costs

cards.title: A good year?
cards.situation: Your stock portfolio rose 8% this year. A broad stock index, the kind you could have bought in one fund, rose 15%. How did you do?

visual.title: This year
visual.label: Over the year the index rises 15% and your portfolio 8%

options.feedback: A gain isn’t the whole story. The extra work earned less than the easy option.

options.text: You lagged the index by 7 points
options.feedback: A gain only looks good next to what you could have had.

options.text: Better: any gain is a win
options.feedback: A gain can still trail the easy option. One index fund would have made 15%.

cards.work: 8% − 15% = −7 points. A simple index fund would have made $700 more on $10,000.
cards.added: Feedback for C written for the Academy

cards.title: Pick a benchmark
cards.text: A **[[benchmark|benchmark]]** is an index that matches what you hold. It’s the bar your results must clear.

blocks.tip: Compare like with like: a stock portfolio against a stock index, not against cash.

cards.title: Count every cost
cards.text: You made 12% on your picks. The index fund made 11%. Then come fund fees, trading fees and spreads.

items.title: Your year
items.label: Your year: +12% before costs, +10% after costs; the index fund +11%

cards.foot: Before costs you beat the index. After costs you lagged it. Only the after-cost number counts.

cards.title: Keep score honestly
cards.text: Judge over **years, not weeks**. One great month can be luck. Three years against the right index tells you far more.

cards.title: Did you beat it?
cards.q: You made 10% before costs and paid 1.5% in fees and trading costs. The index fund returned 9% after its own fee. Did you beat it?

options.feedback: 10% is before costs. Take the costs off first, then compare.
After costs you made 8.5%, just under the index fund’s 9%.
That adds the costs instead of taking them off. Costs come out of your return.
They can: both are after-cost returns once you take your 1.5% off.

cards.work: 10% − 1.5% = 8.5%. The index: 9%. You lagged by 0.5 point.
cards.added: Feedback for the options the board doesn’t show written for the Academy

cards.title: The right bar
cards.q: Your portfolio holds large US companies. Which benchmark fits best?

options.feedback: Large stocks belong next to a large-stock index: same kind of assets, same risks.
A savings rate carries almost no risk, so beating it says little. Large stocks belong next to a large-stock index.
Gold is a different asset with its own drivers. Compare like with like.
A friend’s returns could be luck, or a different mix. Use an index that matches what you hold.

lines: Compare with an index that matches what you hold.
